summary: Defines MIB objects for managing GSMP. It is a standards-track document.

eli5.summary: This gives network tools a standard way to check on GSMP.

questions: how do i configure gsmp sessions with snmp
what notifications does the gsmp mib define
subtitle: The SNMP MIB that lets network managers configure and monitor GSMP sessions between switch controllers and label switches.

tldr.problem: GSMP lets a controller operate a label switch, but operators also need a standard way to set up and watch GSMP sessions with network management tools.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines an SMIv2 MIB module with tables for switch controller entities, switch entities, ATM and TCP/IP encapsulation settings and live sessions, plus notifications for session and port events.
tldr.outcome: Managers get one standard set of objects for GSMP across vendors. The RFC has since been updated by RFC 9141.

today: RFC 3295 is a Proposed Standard that has been updated by RFC 9141. It has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: What the MIB Covers
sections.content:
RFC 3295 defines a portion of the Management Information Base (MIB) for managed objects of the General Switch Management Protocol (GSMP), as defined in RFC 3292. GSMP is a general purpose protocol to control a label switch: a controller can establish and release connections across the switch, manage ports, and request configuration information or statistics, and the switch can report asynchronous events such as a link going down.

GSMP is asymmetric, with the controller as master and the switch as slave. One controller can run the protocol over separate control connections to many switches, and one switch can be controlled by more than one controller through partitioning. Each (switch controller, switch partition) adjacency is a session, and the MIB provides objects to set up and to monitor these sessions.

It is a protocol MIB. It does not expose information learned through GSMP such as full port configuration, and it leaves out how virtual and physical switch entities relate and how partitions are managed.
sections.eli5: A boss computer can tell a switch where to send traffic. This list lets a person set up that boss-and-worker pairing and check on it, but not see everything the worker knows.

sections.title: The SNMP Management Framework
sections.content:
The RFC follows the usual boilerplate for MIB documents. It describes the SNMP Management Framework as five components: an architecture, a Structure of Management Information (SMIv1 and SMIv2), message protocols (SNMPv1, SNMPv2c and SNMPv3), protocol operations, and a set of fundamental applications with view-based access control.

Managed objects are reached through a virtual information store, the MIB. This memo specifies a module compliant with SMIv2. A SMIv1 version can be produced through translation and must be semantically equivalent, except where objects or events are omitted because no translation is possible, for example for Counter64.
sections.eli5: There is already a standard way for network tools to ask devices questions. This document just writes down the new questions to use for GSMP.

sections.title: Tables and Groups
sections.content:
Two tables configure potential sessions: gsmpControllerTable when acting as a controller and gsmpSwitchTable when acting as a switch. Each row is keyed by a 48-bit entity ID, unique within the operational context of the device. A MAC address MAY be used, and with Ethernet encapsulation the entity ID MUST be the IEEE 802 MAC address of the interface used for the session.

The encapsulation is defined first. For ATM a row goes in gsmpAtmEncapTable (interface, VPI and VCI), and for TCP/IP a row goes in gsmpTcpIpEncapTable (address type, address and port number, with default port 6068). Ethernet needs no extra configuration. Then the entity row is created, and when its row status becomes active the GSMP adjacency protocol starts. All GSMP managers SHOULD follow this creation order, to avoid clashes between multiple managers.

Entity rows hold adjacency parameters: the maximum supported GSMP version, the time between periodic adjacency messages (gsmpControllerTimer and gsmpSwitchTimer, in units of 100 ms with default 10), port and instance numbers, partition settings and a notification map. Controllers also have a resynchronisation setting, and switches have a switch name, a switch type and a suggested window size for unacknowledged request messages.

The gsmpSessionTable shows sessions that are established or being established, with the peer, the negotiated parameters and statistics. A session is a switch controller entity and switch entity pair. Entities configured by other means, such as a command line, SHOULD also appear in these tables.
sections.eli5: There is one form for the boss side and one for the worker side, and a third sheet that shows each live conversation. You fill in how they talk (cable type), then who they are, and then they start.

sections.title: Encapsulations, Textual Conventions and Extension
sections.content:
The encapsulation data is further specified in RFC 3293. The MIB MAY be extended with new standard or proprietary encapsulation types. A new type SHOULD be a new table indexed by the entity ID, and a row in it SHOULD be created before any entity row that uses it.

Five textual conventions are defined: GsmpNameType, GsmpLabelType, GsmpVersion, GsmpPartitionType and GsmpPartitionIdType. The name is a 48-bit quantity, and the partition ID is an 8-bit quantity whose format GSMP does not define. A label is a type-length-value with a 2 octet type and a 2 octet length. Version numbers 1, 2 and 3 map to GSMPv1.1, GSMPv2.0 and GSMPv3. Textual conventions only help human readers and do not change the SMI or SNMP.

The partition type object takes noPartition, fixedPartitionRequest or fixedPartitionAssigned. Session state objects use null, synsent, synrcvd and estab.
sections.eli5: Special name tags make the numbers easier for people to read, but the computers still send plain numbers. If a new cable type shows up, you add one new sheet for it.

sections.title: Notifications
sections.content:
The module defines ten notifications for status changes: gsmpSessionDown (also reports final accounting statistics), gsmpSessionUp, gsmpSendFailureInd, gsmpReceivedFailureInd, gsmpPortUpEvent, gsmpPortDownEvent, gsmpInvalidLabelEvent, gsmpNewPortEvent, gsmpDeadPortEvent and gsmpAdjacencyUpdateEvent.

Each entity has a notification map, a bitmap that switches each of these on or off. The default sends session up and down and the two failure indications. The RFC presents the map as a complement to the filter in the SNMP notification originator, not a duplicate, because GSMP events and SNMP notifications can run on different timescales. For example, in an ATM switch the invalid label event could cause mass SNMP notification flooding if mapped to a notification.
sections.eli5: The switch can ring a bell when something happens. You get a row of on-off switches to pick which events ring it, so the bell does not go off thousands of times a second.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC says that, assuming secure network management such as SNMPv3 is implemented, the objects in this MIB do not pose a threat to network security. Objects with read-write or read-create access may be sensitive, and SET operations without protection can harm network operations.

Some objects may hold sensitive information. They are in gsmpControllerTable and gsmpSwitchTable, so even GET access should be controlled and values possibly encrypted in transit. SNMPv1 by itself is not a secure environment. Implementers are advised to consider SNMPv3, specifically the User-based Security Model (RFC 2574) and the View-based Access Control Model (RFC 2575). It is the operator's responsibility to configure the SNMP entity so only legitimate principals can read or change these objects.
sections.eli5: These dials can change how a network works, so only trusted people should be allowed to turn them. The newer, safer version of SNMP is recommended.
